headline: US-Iran ceasefire collapses; oil surges ~10% over two sessions, the 10-year yield hits its highest since mid-May, and equity futures attempt a modest pre-market bounce.
stance: Risk-off in rates, cautious bounce in equities. Trump declared the Iran ceasefire "over" at the NATO summit in Ankara, triggering fresh US strikes, an Iranian oil-sales waiver revocation, and Strait of Hormuz shipping threats. That two-day energy shock is now feeding directly into inflation expectations (1-year US CPI expectations at 3.7%) and bond markets, with the 10-year yield touching ~4.59% overnight — its highest since mid-May — as markets price in at least one Fed rate hike by year-end. Equity futures are inching higher pre-market (+0.3% S&P, +0.5% NDX, +0.2% Dow), suggesting investors are treating Wednesday's Dow selloff as an over-reaction, but the inflation-via-oil channel remains the dominant headwind into the open.

news.head: Iran ceasefire declared over
news.body: Trump told the NATO summit in Ankara that "as far as I'm concerned, it's over," threatening additional strikes and a new blockade; the US military confirmed a second consecutive day of strikes on Iran and revoked Iran's license to sell crude on global markets.

news.head: Strait of Hormuz threat level raised to 'severe'
news.body: Iran attacked US military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait, and a US-led naval coalition raised the Hormuz threat level to "severe" after Iranian attacks on commercial tankers including a Qatari LNG carrier and a Saudi oil tanker.

news.head: FOMC minutes: hawkish lean, divided committee
news.body: June meeting minutes showed only a few policymakers favored an outright rate hike, but officials expressed growing inflation concern; rate futures now show ~70% probability of a September hike, up from 58% the prior day.

news.head: PepsiCo Q2 earnings before the bell
news.body: PepsiCo reports Q2 2026 this morning (consensus EPS ~$2.21) as the unofficial Q2 earnings-season opener; multiple analysts have cut price targets ahead of results, citing Frito-Lay North America volume uncertainty.

news.head: Weekly jobless claims & existing home sales
news.body: Weekly initial claims (8:30 AM ET) and existing home sales (10:00 AM ET) are today's macro data points; the prior 4-week moving average of claims stood at 222K, a healthy labor-market signal.

news.head: Tech staged a partial recovery overnight
news.body: European and Asian tech stocks bounced Thursday after Wednesday's chip-sector rout; Nasdaq 100 futures are up ~0.5% pre-market and SK Hynix shares rose 5.3% in Asia.

news.head: China PPI accelerates; CPI softens
news.body: China's factory-gate inflation (PPI) rose 4.1% year-on-year in June — the fastest pace since July 2022 — while consumer prices rose only 1.0%, adding a disinflationary consumer backdrop alongside reflationary producer prices.

news.head: Trump targets Spain at NATO
news.body: Trump said he wanted to "cut off all trade with Spain" at the NATO summit, sending Spanish bonds lower and adding a fresh trade-war risk layer to European markets.

implications: Higher oil prices flowing through to inflation expectations (3.7% one-year CPI expectations) tighten the path for the Fed: the June FOMC minutes confirmed a hawkish lean, and markets are now pricing at least one hike by year-end — bad for rate-sensitive sectors like real estate, small-caps, and consumer credit.

The 10-year yield (PRIOR CLOSE: 4.56%; overnight: ~4.59%) is at its highest since mid-May; real rates remain elevated at 2.31%, compressing the equity risk premium further — the ERP is already negative at -2.05%, meaning bonds now offer a better risk-adjusted return than stocks on a blended basis.

Oil's two-day surge (~10%) is a direct tailwind for energy stocks but a headwind for transport, consumer staples, and discretionary — watch PepsiCo's guidance today for the first read on margin pass-through under elevated input costs.
Rotation continues: money is moving out of AI/chip leaders (which are breaking 50-day moving averages) and into healthcare, financials, and energy — the internal breadth divergence is widening.

Positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left on Nasdaq 100 futures (1st percentile of 3 years) and Russell 2000 (2nd percentile) — a contrarian floor that argues against aggressive shorting of equities even as macro deteriorates. Copper specs are at the opposite extreme: extended long at the 95th percentile — a contrarian warning for industrial metals. British pound specs are at their most extended short in three years (1st percentile) — a contrarian floor for GBP.

watch.head: PepsiCo Q2 print (~7 AM ET)
watch.body: Full-year guidance and Frito-Lay volume trends are the swing factors; a miss on guidance could weigh on the entire consumer-staples sector given already-lowered targets from JPMorgan, UBS, Barclays, and Bernstein.

watch.head: Weekly jobless claims (8:30 AM ET)
watch.body: The prior 4-week average sits at 222K; any significant deterioration would complicate the Fed's hike narrative and could provide a short-term rally catalyst for bonds.

watch.head: Crude oil intraday direction
watch.body: WTI (PRIOR CLOSE: $74.76/bbl) is trading with a slight overnight bid; a sustained move above ~$75-76 could reignite inflation fears and pressure the equity bounce, while a fade would ease yields.

watch.head: 10-year yield (overnight ~4.59%)
watch.body: Watch whether the yield holds below the 4.60% threshold flagged by bond traders as the next psychological resistance; a break higher would accelerate rotation out of growth/tech.

watch.head: USD/JPY (PRIOR CLOSE: 162.54¥/$)
watch.body: The yen is at the 99.9th percentile of its 3-year range — extreme weakness — raising the probability of Bank of Japan intervention; any sudden yen strengthening would hit dollar-denominated assets broadly.

watch.head: SpaceX joins Nasdaq 100
watch.body: SpaceX's addition to the Nasdaq 100 index is scheduled; passive-fund rebalancing flows could create intraday technical distortions in NDX components.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: 10-year Treasury yield (PRIOR CLOSE: 4.56%; overnight: ~4.59%) is at its highest since mid-May, driven by oil-induced inflation repricing and hawkish FOMC minutes.
2-year yield (PRIOR CLOSE: 4.21%) keeps the yield curve (2s/10s) in positive territory at +35 bps — meaning longer-term borrowing costs exceed short-term rates, a mildly normalizing curve signal.
Real rates (inflation-adjusted 10-year yield) stand at 2.31% — that is the actual cost of money after stripping out expected inflation, and it remains historically restrictive for risk assets.

10-year breakeven inflation (what bond markets expect CPI to average over a decade) sits at 2.25% (PRIOR CLOSE), but near-term 1-year CPI expectations have moved to 3.7% — a meaningful gap that signals short-term oil shock fear rather than entrenched long-run inflation.
FOMC minutes confirmed only a few policymakers wanted to hike in June, but committee-wide inflation concern is growing; rate futures now imply ~70% odds of a September hike, up from 58% pre-minutes.
Bond market volatility (MOVE index: 72.4) is relatively contained — the bond market is not panicking, just repricing gradually upward.

Fed balance sheet is barely growing (+0.98% YoY); overnight reverse repo (RRP) has drained to just $3.3 billion, meaning excess cash that once padded markets is nearly gone — liquidity is tighter at the margin.
Financial conditions indices (ANFCI: -0.506; STLFSI: -0.72) remain in loosely accommodative territory despite the yield rise, suggesting systemic stress is not yet elevated.
sections.positioning: In rates futures, speculators have almost no bullish bets left on 3-month SOFR (1st percentile of 3 years) — a contrarian-bullish lean suggesting the market may be over-positioned for rate hikes in short maturities.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: S&P 500 (PRIOR CLOSE: 7,482.71) futures are up ~0.3% pre-market, attempting to recoup Wednesday's Dow-led selloff; Nasdaq 100 (PRIOR CLOSE: 25,870.65) futures +~0.5% pre-market.
Dow Jones (PRIOR CLOSE: 52,348.39) dropped 576 points (1.09%) Wednesday — the sharpest single-session decline in weeks — as energy-stock gains failed to offset broad selling in rate-sensitive names.
Breadth is narrowing: only 60.2% of S&P 500 stocks trade above their 50-day moving average and 65.1% above their 200-day — healthy but softening from recent peaks.
Nasdaq 100 breadth mirrors this: 55.4% above the 50-day, 63.4% above the 200-day — the tech complex is showing internal fatigue even as the headline index held up better than the Dow on Wednesday.

Valuation remains stretched: the Shiller CAPE ratio (a smoothed price-to-earnings measure using the last 10 years of earnings) stands at 41.64 — well above historical averages — leaving little margin of safety if earnings disappoint.

Rotation narrative: money has moved from AI/chip leaders (breaking 50-day MAs) into healthcare, financials, energy, transports, and insurance — the question is whether rotation can sustain the index or whether selling eventually broadens.
VIX (PRIOR CLOSE: 16.9) remains benign; speculators hold a net short VIX position (12th percentile) — a contrarian-bullish equity lean, as market participants are not aggressively buying protection.

Copper (PRIOR CLOSE: $6.1075/lb; 94th percentile of 3-year range) — an economy-sensitive metal — remains at extreme elevated levels, suggesting industrial demand expectations are still robust despite geopolitical noise.
sections.positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left on Nasdaq 100 futures (4th percentile, 3-year low) and Russell 2000 futures (2nd percentile) — both sit at contrarian floors. Large off-exchange block buying (quiet institutional accumulation) and a burst of unusual options buying are both live on CarMax (KMX) and Scorpio Tankers (STNG) — the highest-conviction fresh setups on today's scan.

single_name.note: Scorpio Tankers (STNG) — product tanker operator directly exposed to Hormuz rerouting premium: company insiders have been buying (2 insider rules fired), large off-exchange block buying is live, a burst of unusual options buying is active, shorts are moderately heavy at 4.0 days to cover (some squeeze risk), and price trades above its 200-day moving average. Signal is fresh.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: High-yield credit spread over investment-grade (HY/IG spread: 267 bps) — this measures how much extra yield junk-rated borrowers must pay versus safer companies — remains within a normal range, suggesting corporate credit markets are not yet pricing in recession risk.
Investment-grade option-adjusted spread (IG OAS: 76 bps) is similarly contained; credit stress is not flashing red even as equity volatility ticks up.
The ratio of high-yield to investment-grade ETF prices (1.3516) is stable — junk bonds are holding their value relative to higher-quality bonds, a sign that credit investors are not fleeing risk.
FRA-OIS and SOFR-OIS spreads (both at -1 bp) — these measure banking-system stress — are essentially flat, confirming no interbank funding stress.
Commercial paper funding spread (CPFF: 21 bps) — the cost for large companies to borrow short-term — is modest and normal.
Bank credit growth (+6.33% YoY) and syndicated loan yields (6.95%) show lending is still expanding at a healthy pace.
M2 money supply is growing at 5.58% YoY — above its long-run average — providing a moderate liquidity tailwind to asset prices.
Treasury General Account (TGA: $880.2bn) remains large; as Treasury spends down this cash pile it injects liquidity into the banking system — a technical positive for market plumbing.
